lead: Spark timing is the instant the plug fires. Spark advance, also called ignition advance, is how many crank degrees before top dead centre (TDC) the spark occurs. The flame needs time to burn the charge, so the spark must come early enough for peak pressure to arrive just after TDC. As speed rises the same burn time covers more crank degrees, so advance must rise; at high load it must fall to avoid knock. Only a few syllabi list this as a separate topic, but every petrol engine uses it.
prereq: You need: Ignition systems: battery and magneto and Electronic ignition.

blocks.text: Spark advance θ is the crank angle before TDC at which the spark fires. Combustion takes time: the flame grows from the plug and pressure rises. Peak pressure should arrive about 10° to 15° after TDC for best torque. If the spark is late, the piston is already moving down and pressure is wasted; if it is too early, pressure peaks before TDC, the piston works against it and the end gas may knock.

blocks.where: θ is the advance (° before TDC); N is the speed (rpm); t<sub>b</sub> is the time from spark to peak pressure (s); θ<sub>pk</sub> is the target peak position (° after TDC). 6N is the crank speed in degrees per second.

blocks.text: The burn time is not fixed: more turbulence at higher speed makes the flame faster, so t<sub>b</sub> falls, and the advance rises with speed but less than in proportion. The advance that gives the most torque is called MBT timing.

Older distributors used centrifugal and vacuum advance. Centrifugal weights move outward with speed and turn the cam or reluctor ahead. The vacuum unit adds advance at part load, where the charge is diluted by leftover exhaust gas and has low density, so it burns slowly. Many engines take ported vacuum from just above the throttle, which is near zero at idle and at wide-open throttle, so vacuum advance drops away at full load.

Modern engines use an ECU spark map of advance against speed and load (from manifold pressure or air flow). A knock sensor, a piezo accelerometer on the block, detects knock; the ECU retards that cylinder a few degrees, then advances back slowly. To check base timing:

items: Warm the engine and set the specified idle speed.
Disconnect and plug the vacuum hose if the maker states it.
Find the fixed pointer on the timing cover and the mark on the crank pulley.
Clip the timing light's pickup on the number one plug lead; aim the flashing light at the marks and read the advance.
Compare the reading with the specification and turn the distributor to correct it.

blocks.text: High load needs less advance to avoid knock; light load needs more because the diluted charge burns slowly.

figure.caption: The worked example on a crank-angle scale. With peak pressure held at 14° after TDC, the 4.0 ms burn at 1500 rpm needs a spark at 22°; at 3000 rpm turbulence cuts the burn to 2.5 ms, so 31° is enough, while a burn that stayed at 4.0 ms would need 58°.

spec.aria: Three crank-angle bars ending at 14 degrees after TDC. At 1500 rpm the spark is 22 degrees before TDC; at 3000 rpm with a 2.5 millisecond burn it is 31 degrees; a dashed bar shows that a 4.0 millisecond burn at 3000 rpm would need 58 degrees.

examples.question: At 1500 rpm the time from spark to peak pressure is 4.0 ms; at 3000 rpm more turbulence cuts it to 2.5 ms. Peak pressure should be 14° after TDC. Find the spark advance at both speeds, and the advance that 3000 rpm would need if the burn time had stayed at 4.0 ms.
steps: At 1500 rpm the crank turns 6 × 1500 = 9000 °/s; spark to peak = 9000 × 0.0040 = 36°; θ = 36° − 14° = 22° before TDC.
With 4.0 ms at 3000 rpm: 18 000 × 0.0040 = 72°; θ = 72° − 14° = 58°, an impossible advance.
examples.answer: 22° at 1500 rpm and 31° at 3000 rpm. Doubling the speed raised the advance by only 9°, because turbulence shortened the burn time.

traps: Advance is not fixed; high load needs retard, even at the same speed, to avoid knock.
10° advance means 10° before TDC, not after.
Centrifugal advance follows speed; vacuum advance follows load through manifold vacuum.
In θ = 6Nt<sub>b</sub> − θ<sub>pk</sub>, N is in rpm and t in seconds; using ms or 360N gives answers far too large.
Knock-sensor retard is temporary protection; the ECU then advances back.

quiz.a: Crank angle before TDC at which the spark fires.

quiz.q: Why does advance rise with speed?
quiz.a: The burn takes a time, and at higher speed that time covers more crank degrees, so the spark must start earlier. Turbulence shortens the burn, so the rise is less than proportional.

quiz.q: At 2000 rpm the spark-to-peak time is 3.0 ms and the peak should be 12° after TDC. Find the advance.
Why does high load need less advance than low load?
quiz.a: At high load the charge is dense and hot, the end gas is closer to auto-ignition, and too early a spark makes it knock; retarding the spark lowers peak pressure and temperature.

quiz.q: A knock sensor retards timing. State one benefit and one cost.
quiz.a: Benefit: stops knock and protects the engine. Cost: lower power and higher exhaust temperature.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production ECUs add knock control and sometimes ion-current or cylinder-pressure feedback to hold MBT timing. Search for spark advance map and knock control loop.
